solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: He's daft … I'm oddly clumsy

indicators.note: done oddly means done in a strange way, so the letters before it are put into a strange order

blocks.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone admits their partner is daft and they themselves are strangely clumsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' sounds as if it describes the clumsiness, but it is the signal to rearrange He's daft I'm into HAM-FISTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham-fisted is an informal adjective for someone who handles things awkwardly, a close synonym of clumsy.

clue.text: Dislike what everybody shows

indicators.note: the words that follow display the answer within them, as a shop window shows its goods

blocks.note: sits across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A question of how people display their aversion to something.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate is to feel strong aversion, so it stands as a verb for dislike.

clue.text: Wine produced in restricted amounts at first

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of each of the preceding words

blocks.note: produced means made
the initials of the three words

explanation.surface: A wine that is only made in small, limited quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeira is a fortified wine from the Portuguese island of the same name.

clue.text: Wicked leaders of industry love lay-offs

indicators.note: the leaders of a group of words are the letters at the front of each

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Bosses in business who enjoy sacking workers are wicked.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill can mean evil or harmful, as in ill deeds or ill will, a sense matching wicked.

clue.text: Go home and go to bed

blocks.note: a go in a game is your turn
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A tired person's plan for the evening: get back to the house and sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go home' reads as one action, but each word stands alone: a go in a game is your turn, and someone at home is in.
explanation.definitionFit: Turn in is an informal phrasal verb meaning to retire for the night, the same as going to bed.

clue.text: Outlaw ridiculous road speed

indicators.note: something ridiculous is absurd and disordered, so the letters after it are jumbled

blocks.note: the nine letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A criminal who drives at an absurdly high speed on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless criminal, a Wild West word for a bandit or outlaw.

clue.text: Middle part of the passport possibly covered up

indicators.note: the middle part of a word is the letter at its centre

blocks.note: the central letter of this three-letter word
a passport is one example of identification; possibly marks it as an example

explanation.surface: Part of someone's passport has been concealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The passport' looks like a single phrase, but 'Middle part of' acts on 'the' alone, leaving the passport as ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Hid is the past tense of hide, so it means concealed or covered up.

clue.text: Divide things equally, or be obliged to accept 50

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: as in have to, meaning must
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A choice between splitting things fairly or being forced to take fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: HAVE takes L inside it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To halve something is to split it into two equal parts, the action of dividing equally.

clue.text: Senior academic had to give money

blocks.note: a don is a senior university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge
had as in had dinner

explanation.surface: A senior university teacher was forced to hand over cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had to' reads as 'was obliged to', but 'had' is ate, as in had a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to contribute funds to a cause, which is giving money.

clue.text: Roofer accepting two days will create something insignificant

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the first piece wraps around what follows

blocks.note: a roofer may lay tiles
D is the abbreviation for day, twice

explanation.surface: A roofer who agrees to a two-day job will produce something trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will create' is only a link; the roofer is the outer piece wrapped round the two days.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiddler is British slang for a small fish or child, hence anything small and unimportant.

clue.text: To some extent, it's a long-forgotten beauty spot?

indicators.note: to some extent means only partly, so just a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: runs across the ends and start of these words

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a scenic place has long been forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in itS A LONg. A beauty spot is normally scenic countryside; the question mark allows a punning reading as a place for beauty treatments.
explanation.definitionFit: A beauty salon is where hair and cosmetic treatments are done, a spot for beauty in a pun on the scenic phrase.

clue.text: New tier assigned as prime viewing space

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so the letters that follow are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: the twelve letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A new row of seats is allocated as the best spot for watching.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringside seat is right by a boxing ring or circus ring, the best place to watch the action.

clue.text: Metalworker requires light mods to be re-tweaked

indicators.note: to tweak again is to adjust once more, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A craftsman needs some minor modifications to be adjusted again.
explanation.definitionFit: A goldsmith works gold into jewellery and objects, a kind of metalworker.

clue.text: Cry with pain

blocks.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
an ail is an archaic noun for an ailment or trouble

explanation.surface: Someone shouting out because they are hurting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cry with pain' reads as a single phrase, but 'Cry' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A wail is a long high-pitched cry of grief or pain, so it means cry as noun or verb.

clue.text: A bully occasionally dismissed in a deft manner

indicators.note: letters thrown out every so often leave only every other one behind

blocks.note: taken as written
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A bully is sometimes sent away skilfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Ably means with skill or competence, the adverb matching a deft manner.

clue.text: Support friend without breaking the law

blocks.note: a leg supports a table or chair
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Backing up a friend while staying within the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Legally means in accordance with law, the adverb for acting without breaking it.

clue.text: As stated, you look for a place in Africa

indicators.note: as stated means as spoken out, so the answer matches the sound of the words that follow

blocks.note: gander is informal for a look, as in take a gander

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to search for somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Gander is informal British and American slang for a look; 'you gander' said quickly matches the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa, so it is one place on that continent.

clue.text: A snooty type upset over current style of Japanese art

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the words read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a snob is a snooty person
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An arrogant person grows annoyed about the latest trend in Japanese art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places the reversed piece above I in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonsai is the Japanese art of growing miniature trees in pots, a style of Japanese art.

clue.text: Artist profits, having place for market in London

blocks.note: gains are profits
Borough Market is a famous food market in Southwark, London

explanation.surface: A painter makes money from a pitch at a London market.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gainsborough was an 18th-century English portrait and landscape painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gainsborough was a celebrated English painter, so his name serves for an artist.

clue.text: Yellow-white gold surrounded by green leaves?

indicators.note: something surrounded by another lies inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: ivy is a plant with evergreen leaves; the question mark marks the definition by example
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Pale gold surrounded by foliage, like a picture in a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is the heraldic term for gold, a convention crosswords use often.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivory is the creamy yellowish-white colour of elephant tusks.

clue.text: Final parts of chat show were quite sentimental

indicators.note: the final parts of words are the letters at their ends

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: The ending of a talk show was rather mawkish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite' looks like part of the definition, but its last letter is the fourth piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee is a British word for sweetly or excessively quaint and sentimental.

clue.text: I complain about Ruth's mother-in-law

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the preceding words are read backwards

blocks.note: to moan is to complain

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about their mother-in-law from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it reverses I MOAN.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Ruth, Naomi is the mother of Ruth's husband, so she is Ruth's mother-in-law.

clue.text: Everything featured in TV programme is superficial

indicators.note: something featured in a programme appears within it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a television programme is a show
everything is all

explanation.surface: Television that covers everything only skims the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Featured in' tells you the word for everything sits inside the word for a TV programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallow means lacking depth of thought, a direct synonym of superficial.

clue.text: Publicity materials using laddism from time to time

indicators.note: from time to time means now and then, so only every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Marketing that sometimes leans on laddish humour.
explanation.walkthrough: Laddism is British for boorish young-male behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Ads, short for advertisements, are pieces of material made to publicise a product.

clue.text: One unspecified area west of New York

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
the standard abbreviation for the state and city

explanation.surface: A vague location somewhere to the west of New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West of' in an across clue simply puts the first piece to the left of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Any refers to one thing chosen without specifying which, as in pick any card.

clue.text: Bob maybe drunk this early

indicators.note: someone drunk is unsteady and muddled, so the letters after it are mixed up

blocks.note: the nine letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Bob has got drunk at an unusually early hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name, but it is a short haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short haircut level with the jaw, so it is one example of a hairstyle.
